unsettled: The entry does not say whether the measured farmstead yard is read from an Edo-period record or a later survey.

why: This is the class our blue plots belong to, and these entries are what let a reader clicking one of them learn why a wet field is a poorer field rather than simply a wetter one. Which of a settlement's plots are wet is our own placement, made from the ground the map puts them on.

It gives the contrast term for the wet paddy - the dry paddy that drains and can carry a winter crop - and the scale of the Meiji conversion, which is what tells us that much of the premodern paddy was the wet kind. Its limits are that the two-thirds figure is hedged in the source itself as what is commonly said; and that it is a modern figure about a modern program - the entry gives no premodern share of wet paddy, so the step from "two thirds were converted after Meiji" to "a premodern map carries wet paddy" is the record's inference and not the source's statement.

Where our maps run fields up a valley floor, this is the field type they are, and the entry gives both the setting and its character - old, wet, and often rain-fed rather than fed by a channel, which bears on whether we draw a supply ditch to it. We take the character of the ground from it and no dimension.

That plot-to-plot cascade is the behavior our field layouts depend on, and it is a consequence of flat, bunded, gravity-fed paddies rather than of any modern works. The limits are that what we draw from the cascade - which plot ends up wettest - is our own inference, labeled as such where we use it, not something the paper says.

It corroborates the district's own page on the one point the record turns on - channels INSIDE the settlement, feeding a named stream down its center. Its limits are that it cites the designation rather than a survey, it is used here only for what the community's own site already says, and its one date for the arrangement is a hearsay line that kabata already existed in the Yayoi period - which dates the water-huts rather than the layout of the channels, so like the district's own page it is evidence of the FORM and not of its age.

It is cited here as a TRAP rather than as support: its "both sides" modifies a street, not a watercourse, and a reader meeting the term could take it for evidence that settlements straddle streams. It says a linear settlement may FOLLOW a river; it does not say its buildings stand on both banks of one. Its worked examples - in Quebec, Norfolk, Merseyside and Hong Kong - are Western and modern rather than premodern East Asian.

unsettled: The definition is of a farming-village form given with no era, from a 1967 book, so the period table cannot place it.

why: "Mountains on three sides, water on one side" is the cleanest statement read that the ideal village has its water BESIDE it rather than through it. Its limits: it describes an ideal configuration in fengshui terms rather than a surveyed distribution, and it does not say which bank the houses occupy in fact - it names the village's old stone arch bridge as its main entrance without saying what water it crosses; the phrase itself is the 2020 authors' summary of the site rather than a period text, so it dates the reading and not the village.
unsettled: The village is traditional but the evidence is a 2020 reading of it, so premodern versus present-day is a judgment.

why: Its recurring verbs are the evidence: streams that flow AROUND AND PAST a village, on a named side. The two worked cases differ in strength - Wanfu has a stream on each side flowing around and past it, while Shenquan's runs west of the village and through the whole of its DOMAIN before reaching the river below, which says less than the first. Its limits: the analysis is of ideal configurations as much as surveyed fact, and the paper states no case of a village divided by its own stream - an absence, which is weaker than a statement. Two more limits travel with it: its sample spans three regions and building traditions, from northern Shaanxi's cliff cave-dwellings to southern Shaanxi's courtyard and stone-slab houses (Wanfu, the village quoted here, is in the south); and the 35 villages are heritage-listed survivors chosen for typicality, so they are a selection rather than a distribution.
unsettled: The villages are traditional but the evidence is a 2017 survey of them, so premodern versus present-day is a judgment.

why: It describes an eighteenth-century Japanese irrigation scheme in the geometry our water layouts use - two supply canals carried high along the plateau rims on either side, and the river draining the lowland between - and it comes from the city that keeps the site. Its limits are that it describes one Kanto system as it survives; and that it gives the geometry only - that the fields could be fed from either side is our reading of that geometry, not the page's words.

We use it for that grid module and its proportions, which is the frame our regular field patterns are laid out on and the reason a long-settled plain reads as ruled rather than as a patchwork. Its limits: it is a translation rather than the Japanese original; and jori was an ancient state land system whose regularity survived only where the ground and the centuries allowed, so a grid this tidy suits a broad old plain and not every valley we draw.

It gives the small end of a really worked paddy - basins of a few square meters, the smallest a quarter of one - which is what tells us that no absolute minimum paddy area exists and lets our steepest fields be drawn tiny. Its limits are that it is an extreme case, basins made tiny by a steep slope, so it is a floor and never a typical size; and that its counts describe the terrace's present state, not a documented historical layout - and the page gives the average and the minimum only, so how many basins run about a square meter is our reading, not its figure.

It supplies the physical distinction our terraced maps depend on, that the tall riser is a retaining wall holding up the soil while a separate low lip holds in the water, which is why micro-basins belong on a hillside and not on a valley floor. The clear limitation is place: these are Himalayan terraces in Nepal standing in for East Asian ones because no comparable published measurements of Japanese or Chinese terrace risers could be read on a public page; and parts of its text are automatically compiled, so we use it for the geometry of the structure and not for the details of how it is farmed.

It gives us a real, counted case of how much land a cluster of small farm ponds waters and how many households share it - one ward's systems serving about fifty hectares for eleven farmers - which is the scale at which we draw a pond against the fields below it. Its own counts of the ward's ponds differ between passages; and it states no typical or maximum command area at all, so the upper bound our maps work to is our guess rather than its finding.

It is an eyewitness account of tea growing before mechanization, before state terracing programs, and before the twentieth century rearranged the hillsides, which makes it about as close to a premodern observation of a tea slope as a readable source gets. The limits are that it is one traveler's narrative written for a Victorian British readership rather than a survey, and that it covers the coastal and northern provinces he happened to pass through.

It is peer-reviewed work about the exact feature we draw. The figure of roughly two fengshui forests per village that we take from it is not the paper's own measurement: it quotes it, for Fujian province as a whole, from a 2012 Chinese study we have not read, so the number reaches us at second hand. It does not give us grove sizes: its own table records whole-village forest areas only, and it counts no trees or canopies, so the per-grove areas on our maps are labeled guesses. It is also a small interview-based study of the groves that survived in one county of one province, so it describes a remnant landscape rather than the ordinary one of several centuries ago.

It carries two statements this record rests on: that rice was domesticated in naturally marshy areas close to rivers, and that a polder is ground reclaimed from a swamp or lake behind a high solid dyke - the origin story the marsh and polder entries assume. Its limits are its genre: a teaching article of a few pages, written out of the author’s own larger scholarship rather than presenting new evidence, so it is a reliable statement of what the field holds and never a measurement.

It gives the plain definition of the thing our maps now draw across a brook at the intake, and the one fact about it a map needs: that the ordinary weir passes water over its crest rather than stopping the stream. Its limits are that it is written about weirs in general and modern ones in particular, with nothing on what a village weir was built of before modern times or where a canal leaves it, so those rest on other sources.

It names the parts of the transition from stream to canal in the order a map draws them, which is what the entry on the intake rests on. Its limits are that it is modern engineering practice, silent on village-built works before modern times and on whether the river continues below the works, so both of those rest on other sources.

It is a Japanese river engineer's account of the intake as a premodern institution, and it names the whole sequence of works - weir, intake mouth, settling basin, division works - which is the sequence our maps follow at the head of a field. Its limits are that its Yayoi date is reported as hearsay ("is said to be seen"), and that it gives no dimensions and no description of any one village weir.

It states in the plainest words read what a diversion weir does and what becomes of the water it does not take - it goes over the crest and on down the river - which is the fact our maps rest on when the brook runs on past the intake.

It is the best-known premodern Chinese case of a river divided rather than taken, with the split stated in numbers, and it grounds the rule that the parent stream keeps flowing below an intake. Its limits are that Dujiangyan is a river-scale state work and not a village brook, and that its weirless form is exceptional rather than typical.

It gives a second premodern division of a river in stated proportions, with the barrier an overflow crest rather than a closure, corroborating the rule that the stream continues below a diversion. Its limits are the same as Dujiangyan's: a river-scale state work, not a village brook.

It shows that the two intake forms our maps roll between - a low weir of stone-filled cribs, or a bare intake off a river bend - are both readings of the same ancient work, and it places the head where the river leaves the hills, as the Japanese rule does. Its limits are that the form is expressly disputed, and that the work is a great state canal rather than a village ditch.

It states plainly that the official lived inside the compound he worked in, which is why the Chinese seat on our maps has no separate magistrate's house. The sentence we rest on sits in a section the article itself marks as citing no sources, so it carries the discount of any uncited encyclopedia line; the Columbia teaching page beside it corroborates the rotation and avoidance rules that made the official an outsider, not the residence itself.

It dates the concentration of the domains' rice trade at Osaka with two counts, which is the attested fact behind our capital's wharf-side granary district. The article carries a notice that it lacks sufficient sources and states the counts as what is said to have been, uncited - the discount that matters most where two numbers are taken - and it says nothing about how much of any domain's rice went there.

It gives the length, the route and the two forms of the channel - open cut outside the city, buried pipe within - which is exactly the division our capital's water supply draws. It is used only for facts its own references and the Edo-Tokyo Museum's exhibition page state as well.

It states in plain English two things the Japanese reference pages state separately - that each samurai estate was its own walled enclosure with one or two gates, and that the commoner city was cut up by thousands of gates that closed at night - and it gives the scale of the block system. Its limits are that its estates are Edo's greatest, not a provincial castle town's.

It gives the count and the manning of the palings, which is the Chinese half of the two-traditions argument our night gates rest on, and it dates the institution to the Ming. Its limits are that Beijing was the imperial capital and the most policed city in the empire, so its counts and manning are an upper bound a provincial town's night gates do not approach.

It says what the block gates were for and who paid for them, from standard reference works rather than a hobby page, and it gives the machi-kido's hours. Its limits are that its hours for the town gate differ from another page this record cites, which the note at that sentence discloses. It is also a great-city account. The Heibonsha entry, signed by Tamai Tetsuo, puts a gate on every block mainly in Edo and Osaka, and one gate for several blocks in small and middle-sized towns. The Yamakawa entry names castle towns, such as Sendai and Matsuyama, that had no gate on each block, only gates at the town's entrances and between the samurai and townsmen quarters. Its hours and the gate's form are Edo's. So a gate on every block fits our cities, and not a smaller town.

It places the emperor's secretariat inside the palace, which is the Chinese half of the rule this page draws - the ruler's council beside the ruler, the executive bureaus outside. It also warns that the body was never a first-rank organ of state.

It supplies the European comparison this page draws - the corner as the weak point of a curtain - and, read fully, it corrects the comparison by calling the weakness theoretical for most of the period.

It gives the length and extent of the largest town enclosure of its age, the exemplar behind our capital's single rampart around the whole population. The article carries a notice asking for its sources; the nine-kilometer sentence itself is uncited, which matters because a map is scaled against it.

It gives the standard layout taxonomy our castle's bailey arrangement is drawn from, and it says which forms follow the terrain. It is the page that shows one of those forms is circular, which keeps this record from calling them all angular.
It describes the surviving Qing yamen's plan in plain terms, the courtyard-and-axis form our maps give the seat of government.
